neighbours.text: Opened in 1983 at 1509 Broadway, Neighbours is Seattle's oldest still-operating LGBTQ+ club, where drag legend Crystal Lane grew the local drag and fundraising scene before her death in 1994.
neighbours.descriptor: Capitol Hill gay dance club on Broadway since 1983

neptune-theatre.text: The Neptune opened as a silent-movie house in 1921 and still wears its sea-god theme, with statues of Neptune and a concession stand shaped like a boat. It screened The Rocky Horror Picture Show weekly for 14 years starting in 1991, among the longest continuous runs in the country, before Seattle Theatre Group spent $700,000 turning it into a live venue in 2011.
neptune-theatre.descriptor: 1921 U District movie palace turned live-music venue, with Neptune statues

nishino.text: Chef Tatsu Nishino, a Kyoto native, trained in Osaka and cooked at Matsuhisa in Los Angeles before opening his own restaurant on East Madison Street in 1995, a short walk from the Washington Park Arboretum.
nishino.descriptor: Madison Park Japanese restaurant and sushi bar, open since 1995

northwest-film-forum.text: It started in 1995 as WigglyWorld Studios, a filmmakers' collective founded on a King County Arts Commission grant, and is now a nonprofit two-screen arthouse on 12th Ave in Capitol Hill, with workshops and youth programs alongside the screenings. Its signature event, the Local Sightings Film Festival, programs nothing but Pacific Northwest filmmakers.
northwest-film-forum.descriptor: Nonprofit two-screen arthouse cinema on 12th Ave, Capitol Hill

nue.text: Nue serves hard-to-find street food from around the world — Latvian smoked sprats, Trinidadian goat curry, Romanian mititei, a Japanese katsu sandwich on white bread with Kewpie mayo — under co-owner Uyên Nguyễn. Atlas Obscura called it one of the most adventurous dining experiences in the Pacific Northwest.
nue.descriptor: Global street-food restaurant on 14th Ave, Capitol Hill

occidental-square.text: Created in 1971 on the former site of the Carrollton Hotel, the Pioneer Square park hosted Seattle's first Pride Week in 1974, when around 200 LGBTQ people gathered for a picnic and dance party; the city made it the Pride parade endpoint in 1977 until the parade moved to Capitol Hill in the 1980s. Hai Ying Wu's Fallen Firefighters Memorial honors four firefighters killed in a 1995 International District warehouse fire.
occidental-square.descriptor: Pioneer Square park with the Fallen Firefighters Memorial

oddfellows-cafe.text: Oddfellows opened in 2008 when Linda Derschang took the ground floor of the Oddfellows Hall, a 1908 Renaissance Revival building by architect C. A. Breitung that served for decades as a cultural nucleus for Capitol Hill's community and arts organizations and still houses the Century Ballroom. Huge communal-style tables set the tone inside.
oddfellows-cafe.descriptor: All-day cafe and bar in the 1908 Oddfellows Hall at 10th & Pine

off-the-rez-cafe.text: Mark McConnell of the Blackfeet Nation and his partner Cecilia Rikard started Off the Rez in 2011 as what the Snoqualmie Valley Record calls Seattle's first Native food truck, then opened this roughly 30-seat cafe inside the Burke Museum on the UW campus in 2019. Bison frybread tacos and wild rice bowls anchor a menu that sources produce, fish and bison from tribal vendors where possible.
off-the-rez-cafe.descriptor: Native American cafe in the Burke Museum, known for bison frybread tacos

olivers-lounge.text: Oliver's opened inside the Mayflower Park Hotel in 1976 as Washington's first "daylight" bar, with street-facing floor-to-ceiling windows. Fifty years on it remains one of Seattle's longest independently owned bars, and the classic martini is still what people come for.
olivers-lounge.descriptor: Martini bar in the Mayflower Park Hotel on Olive Way, downtown, since 1976

olympic-sculpture-park.text: The site belonged to the oil and gas company Unocal until the 1970s and sat as a contaminated brownfield before the Seattle Art Museum cleaned it up and opened the free nine-acre park in January 2007. Works by Alexander Calder, Richard Serra, Louise Bourgeois and Mark di Suvero step down the bluff to a rebuilt beach on Puget Sound.
olympic-sculpture-park.descriptor: Free 9-acre waterfront sculpture park run by the Seattle Art Museum

osteria-la-spiga.text: Chef Sabrina Tinsley and her husband Pietro Borghesi opened la Spiga in 1998 to cook the food of Italy's Emilia-Romagna region. After eight years in a smaller space it moved into Capitol Hill's Piston & Ring building, a converted auto body shop with wooden beams and a long wine-backed bar. The house-made breads are the giveaway: la vera piadina romagnola, gnocco fritto, pane all'olio.
osteria-la-spiga.descriptor: Emilia-Romagna osteria on 12th Ave in a converted auto shop, since 1998

owl-n-thistle.text: Jack Geary and Declan Fury opened the Owl 'N Thistle in 1993 in the Coleman Building, rebuilt after Seattle's Great Fire of 1889; the pub says the foundation is a retired clipper ship, the Windward. A former Scottish proprietress, Bonnie McGregor, gave the place its name. There's live music most nights — trad Irish through jazz and funk — plus pool, darts, Guinness beef stew and fish and chips.
owl-n-thistle.descriptor: Irish pub in the historic Coleman Building with live music most nights

pacific-inn-pub.text: A Stone Way pub that has been frying fish and chips since 1981 and bills itself as "Seattle's Famous Fish & Chips." It's 21-and-over and pours until 2am, which makes it as much a late-night stop as a dinner one.
pacific-inn-pub.descriptor: Fish-and-chips pub on Stone Way in Wallingford, since 1981

pacific-science-center.text: Those arches went up as the United States Science Pavilion for the 1962 World's Fair, designed by Minoru Yamasaki — the architect who later designed New York's World Trade Center. The building stayed on as a science museum and now draws more than a million visitors a year to its IMAX theaters, laser dome, planetarium and butterfly house.
pacific-science-center.descriptor: Hands-on science museum under Yamasaki's arches at Seattle Center

pagliacci-pizza.text: Pagliacci started in 1979 as a single shop in the University District and now runs about two dozen locations in King and Snohomish counties, with Matt Galvin and Pat McDonald as owners. Its boxes have been made from FSC-certified and post-consumer recycled fiber since 2011, and it opened Seattle's first stand-alone LEED-certified pizzeria in Madison Park in 2012.
pagliacci-pizza.descriptor: Seattle pizza chain's West Seattle Junction shop on California Ave SW

palace-kitchen.text: Tom Douglas's third restaurant, open since 1996 and billing itself as a "tavern with good food" — U-shaped bar, dim light, burgers and goat cheese lavender fondue. Eater Seattle called it a centerpiece of Belltown and the late-night industry hangout where cooks and bartenders landed after their shifts. It went dark in March 2020 and stayed closed three years before reopening in April 2023.
palace-kitchen.descriptor: Tom Douglas tavern in Belltown with a U-shaped bar, since 1996

panama-hotel.text: Built in 1910 by Sabro Ozasa, Seattle's first Japanese American architect, the Panama was a hub of Japantown — rooms, shops, restaurants and the Hashidate-Yu bathhouse, one of four sento in early-1900s Seattle and the last one left in the United States. Families stored their belongings in the basement before wartime incarceration and many never came back for them; a glass panel in the floor lets you look down at what's left. National Historic Landmark, 2006.
panama-hotel.descriptor: 1910 Japantown hotel and tea house with an intact basement sento

paramount-theatre.text: It opened in 1928 as the Seattle Theatre and was renamed the Paramount in 1930. The Rapp & Rapp palace still has one of only three original Publix 1 Wurlitzer organs, kept playable by volunteers from the Puget Sound Theatre Organ Society. It joined the National Register in 1974 and became a city landmark in 1995; Nirvana's 1991 concert here was shot on 16mm film.
paramount-theatre.descriptor: 1928 movie palace at 9th and Pine, now a Broadway and concert house

paseo.text: Cuban-born chef Lorenzo Lorenzo opened Paseo in Fremont in 1994, and the garlicky Cuban Roast sandwich drew weekend lines down the block; a 2010 TLC series ranked it the second-best sandwich in America. Both Paseo locations closed abruptly in November 2014 amid bankruptcy, a buyer paid $91,000 for the name at a federal auction, and staff reverse-engineered the recipes to reopen Fremont in January 2015.
paseo.descriptor: Caribbean sandwich counter in Fremont known for the Cuban Roast

pestle-rock.text: Pestle Rock cooks Isan food from Thailand's northeast on Ballard's NW Market Street, and the name is literal — "rocking" the pestle is how the spice pastes that define the region get made. The house line is to eat the way Isan people do: with your hands, mixing and dipping in a range of authentic sauces, because "more messy means more delicious."
pestle-rock.descriptor: Isan (Northeast Thai) kitchen on NW Market Street in Ballard

phnom-penh-noodle-house.text: Sam Ung opened Phnom Penh in 1987 in the Chinatown-International District, starting with seven noodle dishes; it was described in 2020 as Seattle's only Cambodian restaurant. The family closed it in 2018 and reopened after two years in August 2020. Kuyteav and beef lok lak are the dishes it is known for.
phnom-penh-noodle-house.descriptor: Cambodian noodle house on S Jackson St in the C-ID, since 1987

pho-bac.text: Phở Bắc started in 1982 as Cat's Submarine Sandwich Shop until the Vietnamese community talked the owners into serving phở instead. The Pham family has run it ever since and were James Beard semifinalists for Outstanding Restaurateur in 2023; a downtown location opened in 2021 with an upstairs bar called Phởcific Standard Time. The original in the ID is the red boat-shaped building.
pho-bac.descriptor: Downtown outpost of Seattle's Phở Bắc, Vietnamese pho since 1982

pho-bac-sup-shop.text: The Pham family's Phở Bắc started in 1982 as Cat's Submarine Sandwich Shop in the Chinatown–International District; four months after phở went on the menu it had taken over, and the name changed with it. Súp Shop opened on New Year's Day 2018, near the family's original red boat-shaped building on S Jackson St. The Phams were James Beard Outstanding Restaurateur semifinalists in 2023.
pho-bac-sup-shop.descriptor: Phở shop in Little Saigon, from the family behind Seattle's Phở Bắc

pho-than-brothers.descriptor: Pho-only Vietnamese noodle shop near Green Lake, cream puffs for dessert

pike-place-chowder.text: Larry Mellum and Mike Hillyer opened the Post Alley window in 2003, after working up the recipe in the 1990s at a West Seattle cafe. Their New England clam chowder has won repeatedly at chowder cook-offs on both coasts, and the shop counts 17 national chowder titles.
pike-place-chowder.descriptor: Chowder counter in Post Alley at Pike Place Market since 2003

pike-place-market.text: Opened on August 17, 1907, it's one of the oldest continuously operated public farmers markets in the country and Seattle's most-visited attraction, drawing over 20 million people a year. The original Starbucks (1971, moved to 1912 Pike Place in 1977) is here, the Pike Place Fish Market crew still throws salmon over the counter, and a bronze piggy bank named Rachel collects thousands a year for market social services.
pike-place-market.descriptor: Public farmers market above Elliott Bay, open since 1907

pioneer-building.text: Elmer Fisher's Pioneer Building went up in 1892 at 600 First Avenue; when the plans were unveiled in 1888 the local press predicted it would be one of the finest buildings in the country and the largest north of San Francisco. During the 1897 Klondike gold rush, 48 mining companies kept offices inside. It's a National Historic Landmark and the launch point for the Underground Tour.
pioneer-building.descriptor: 1892 Richardsonian Romanesque landmark on First Ave, Pioneer Square

pioneer-square.text: This wedge of brick marks Seattle's original downtown, rebuilt in Richardsonian Romanesque stone and brick after the Great Fire of 1889 and booming as an outfitting hub for the 1897 Klondike gold rush. The 1909 cast-iron-and-glass pergola sheltered cable-car riders and sat atop an underground restroom once called the most lavish west of the Mississippi; it was made a National Historic Landmark in 1977 along with the totem pole and Pioneer Building.
pioneer-square.descriptor: Triangular park at 1st & Yesler with an iron pergola and totem pole

pioneer-square-pergola.text: Built in 1909 by architect Julian Everett, the pergola sheltered cable-car riders and capped an underground public restroom praised at the time as the most lavish west of the Mississippi. A semi-truck destroyed it on January 15, 2001; the city rebuilt it using about 99% original material and reopened it in August 2002. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1977 along with the adjacent Pioneer Building and totem pole.
pioneer-square-pergola.descriptor: 1909 cast-iron and glass cable-car shelter in Pioneer Square

piroshky-piroshky.text: Vladimir and Zina Kotelnikov opened Piroshky Piroshky at Pike Place in 1992, selling savory and sweet Russian hand pies - beef and cheese, chicken pot pie, cinnamon-cardamom braids. Anthony Bourdain filmed there for No Reservations in 2007, and Smithsonian magazine put it on a 2013 list of iconic American food destinations.
piroshky-piroshky.descriptor: Russian piroshky bakery at Pike Place Market since 1992

pony.text: Pony occupies a steel former Associated gas station on E Madison — the bar's own dating puts it in the 1940s, Wikipedia in the 1930s — with a roofed, west-facing patio kept usable year-round by a gas fire pit and electric heaters. It's styled as a tribute to 1970s West Village and Castro bars, and Seattle Weekly readers voted it the city's best gay bar in 2013.
pony.descriptor: Gay dive bar in a converted 1940s gas station on E Madison

poquitos.text: Poquitos opened at 10th and Pike in 2011 under Deming Maclise and James Weimann and has been a Capitol Hill fixture since — Seattle Metropolitan named it one of the best restaurants on the Hill in 2021. The LGBTQ-owned business later expanded to Bothell in 2018 (closed September 2025) and Tacoma in 2022.
poquitos.descriptor: Mexican restaurant at 10th & Pike on Capitol Hill since 2011

port-of-seattle-fishermens-terminal.text: Opened in 1914 on Salmon Bay, it has been the home port of Seattle's commercial fishing fleet ever since, with moorage for more than 700 vessels including boats seen on Deadliest Catch. The Seattle Fishermen's Memorial there carries plaques naming more than 670 local commercial fishermen and women lost at sea since the beginning of the 20th century.
port-of-seattle-fishermens-terminal.descriptor: Port of Seattle home port of the North Pacific fishing fleet on Salmon Bay

portage-bay-cafe.text: Portage Bay Cafe has been doing Seattle breakfast and brunch since 1997, built around a local-organic-sustainable sourcing pledge it sums up as "eat like you give a damn." The South Lake Union café is one of five locations, alongside Roosevelt, Ballard, 65th and West Seattle.
portage-bay-cafe.descriptor: South Lake Union breakfast and brunch spot, organic and local since 1997

portage-bay-cafe-and-catering.text: Portage Bay Cafe started in 1997 on an "eat like you give a damn" premise — local, organic, sustainable — and now runs five Seattle-area cafes. The Roosevelt Way NE location serves the University District, and the house move is ordering house-made pancakes or French toast so you get a run at the fresh toppings bar.
portage-bay-cafe-and-catering.descriptor: Organic breakfast cafe on Roosevelt Way NE with a fresh toppings bar

public-market-clock.text: The clock and red neon 'Public Market Center' sign mark the main entrance to Pike Place Market, which opened August 17, 1907 so shoppers could 'meet the producer' and drew nearly 21 million visitors in 2023 — Seattle's most popular tourist destination. Near the entrance sits Rachel, a 550-pound bronze piggy bank by Georgia Gerber dedicated in 1986; the coins dropped in her fund market social services.
public-market-clock.descriptor: Neon 'Public Market Center' clock over Pike Place Market's main entrance

quinns.text: Scott and Heather Staples opened Quinn's in 2007 as a Capitol Hill take on the 1990s London gastropub; brothers Charles and Peter Kim took it over in 2018. The wild boar sloppy joe is the dish people name first — Eater Seattle put it on a 2014 list of iconic Seattle meat dishes — and Anthony Bourdain filmed here for a 2013 episode of The Layover.
quinns.descriptor: Gastropub at 10th & Pike on Capitol Hill, open since 2007

rachels-ginger-beer-pike-place-market.text: Rachel Marshall was introduced to ginger beer in Germany, started brewing it in Seattle, and sold it at farmers' markets and a Pike Place stall before opening this flagship shop in the Market in July 2013 with partner Adam Peters. Artist Stacey Rozich designed the murals in all four Seattle locations.
rachels-ginger-beer-pike-place-market.descriptor: Fresh-ginger ginger beer shop in Pike Place Market, open since 2013

writtenFor.name: Rachel's Ginger Beer - Pike Place Market

radiator-whiskey.text: Opened in 2013 on the top floor of Pike Place Market's Corner Market building, Radiator Whiskey pairs a deep whiskey list with unapologetically carnivorous cooking — pig's head, pork cheek stew, tater tots — written on a blackboard above an open kitchen. It's a sibling to Matt's in the Market.
radiator-whiskey.descriptor: Whiskey bar and meat-heavy kitchen upstairs in Pike Place Market

rays-boathouse-and-cafe.text: Ray Lichtenberger moved his boat rental and bait business here in 1939, a coffeehouse followed in 1945 and Russ Wohlers made it a full seafood restaurant in 1973; the neon sign dates to 1952. Ray's was one of four places to sell fresh Copper River salmon commercially in 1983 and won a James Beard America's Classics award in 2002. Chris Cornell cooked here before Soundgarden.
rays-boathouse-and-cafe.descriptor: Shilshole Bay seafood restaurant in Ballard

red-mill.text: Red Mill began on Capitol Hill in 1937 as a diner and ice creamery, closed in 1967, and was brought back in 1994 by brothers John and Babe Shepherd, who named it for their late sisters Kathleen and Monica — both had worked at the original. This Interbay shop opened in 1998. The burger has landed on GQ's list of burgers to eat before you die.
red-mill.descriptor: Burgers on W Dravus St in Interbay — Verde burger and pepper bacon, since 1998

red-mill-burgers.text: This is where Red Mill came back. The name goes back to a 1937 Capitol Hill diner and ice creamery that closed in 1967; brothers John and Babe Shepherd reopened it on Phinney Ridge in 1994, naming it for their late sisters Kathleen and Monica, who had worked at the original. It won Seattle Weekly's best burger ten years running, and the Verde — smoky Anaheim chiles, jack cheese, bacon blue cheese — is the one to order.
red-mill-burgers.descriptor: The 1994 original of the revived Red Mill, on N 67th St in Phinney Ridge

revel.text: Chef Rachel Yang opened Revel in Fremont in 2010 and built the room around a big open kitchen fronted by a 26-foot maple butcher-block counter. The cooking is inventive Korean-leaning fusion served as shareable plates.
revel.descriptor: Korean-fusion shared plates in Fremont with an open kitchen, since 2010

rhein-haus-seattle.text: The beer hall opened as Von Trapp's and was renamed Rhein Haus in 2014 to dodge a legal fight over the trademarked Von Trapp name. It pairs bratwurst, schnitzel and giant pretzels with 20 beer taps and bocce courts, and has handed out free pretzels to patrons who show up in lederhosen or a dirndl.
rhein-haus-seattle.descriptor: German beer hall with bocce courts on 12th Ave in Capitol Hill

rob-roy.text: Rob Roy is Anu Apte's Belltown cocktail bar, built around the classics, and it was nominated for the James Beard Foundation's Outstanding Bar award in 2023. Apte also runs its sibling spot, Vinnie's Raw Bar.
rob-roy.descriptor: Classic cocktail bar on 2nd Ave in Belltown

rose-garden.text: Opened in 1924 next to Woodland Park Zoo, the 2.5-acre garden holds roughly 3,000 plants across more than 200 varieties and is free to enter every day from 7:30 a.m. until dusk. It was an accredited All-America Rose Selections test site from 1947 until 2010, and has been grown pesticide-free since 2006.
rose-garden.descriptor: Free 2.5-acre public rose garden beside Woodland Park Zoo

rositas-mexican-grill.text: Opened April 9, 1979 by Sergio Uvence Lopez, his sister Rosa and her husband Wenceslao Anaya, and named for Rosa's childhood nickname. It started small on a then-quiet stretch of Woodlawn and grew into the spaces next door, adding a full bar and a tortilla station; two of the staff have been there more than 40 years.
rositas-mexican-grill.descriptor: Family-run Mexican restaurant on Woodlawn Ave by Green Lake, since 1979

rubinstein-bagels.text: Andrew Rubinstein sold his bagels out of other people's cafés before opening this first bricks-and-mortar shop in the Via6 towers in December 2020. They're sourdough bagels made with 100% organic Pacific Northwest flour; Food & Wine named them among the best bagels in America, and Rubinstein has since sold his stake to Ethan Stowell Restaurants.
rubinstein-bagels.descriptor: Sourdough bagel shop in the Via6 building in South Lake Union

saigon-deli.descriptor: Vietnamese counter-service spot on Brooklyn Ave NE in the U District

saltys.text: Salty's has sat on Harbor Avenue SW for nearly four decades, founded by the local Kingen family — and it opened under the mouthful name Salty Pickerel's & Angus McHereford's, which customers promptly shortened to Salty's. The waterfront setting has drawn OpenTable Diners' Choice nods for scenic views, and Sunday brunch is a buffet.
saltys.descriptor: Waterfront seafood restaurant on Alki's Harbor Ave SW

seattle-aquarium.text: Open on the Elliott Bay piers since 1977, its signature is the Underwater Dome — a 400,000-gallon tank you sit inside while Puget Sound fish circle overhead. The Ocean Pavilion, a nearly 500,000-gallon Coral Triangle habitat, opened in August 2024. About 850,000 people visit each year.
seattle-aquarium.descriptor: Waterfront aquarium on Pier 59 with the Underwater Dome, open since 1977

seattle-art-museum.text: SAM was founded in 1933 and reopened in Robert Venturi's downtown building on First Avenue in December 1991. Jonathan Borofsky's Hammering Man out front had a rough debut: the sculpture fell and was damaged during installation in September 1991 and went back to the foundry, finally rising in 1992. SAM also runs the Olympic Sculpture Park and the Asian Art Museum in Volunteer Park.
seattle-art-museum.descriptor: Downtown art museum at 1300 First Ave, marked by the Hammering Man

seattle-asian-art-museum.text: The 1933 Art Deco building by Carl F. Gould was the Seattle Art Museum's original home until the collection moved downtown in 1991; it reopened as the Seattle Asian Art Museum in 1994. A $56 million renovation closed it from 2017 to 2020, adding a three-story glass-and-sandstone wing behind the preserved historic facade.
seattle-asian-art-museum.descriptor: Art Deco museum of Asian art in Volunteer Park, Capitol Hill

seattle-center.text: The whole 74-acre campus is what the 1962 Century 21 World's Fair left behind — the Space Needle, the Monorail and the science pavilion were all fair structures the city kept and has run since 1963. Pioneer David Denny donated part of the land in 1886 on the condition it stay in public use forever. It now holds Climate Pledge Arena, MoPOP, McCaw Hall and festivals like Bumbershoot and Northwest Folklife.
seattle-center.descriptor: 74-acre 1962 World's Fair campus around the Space Needle

seattle-childrens-museum.text: Started in 1979 with a single exhibit, the museum now fills roughly 18,000 square feet on the lowest floor of the Seattle Center Armory with 11 exhibits aimed at kids from six months to eight years old. The open well visitors peer down into from the Armory's main floor was once part of the Bubbleator, a ride that no longer operates.
seattle-childrens-museum.descriptor: Hands-on play museum under the Seattle Center Armory, founded 1979

seattle-childrens-theater.text: Founded in 1975 out of the volunteer-run Poncho Theatre at Woodland Park Zoo, SCT grew into the second-largest professional children's theatre in the country before moving to Seattle Center in 1993. It plays two houses there — the 482-seat Charlotte Martin Theatre and the 274-seat Eve Alvord — and has built its name on commissioning new work, with 120 of its first 269 plays world premieres.
seattle-childrens-theater.descriptor: Professional theatre for young audiences at Seattle Center, founded 1975

seattle-great-wheel.text: Opened June 29, 2012 on Pier 57, the 175-foot Great Wheel was the tallest Ferris wheel on the US West Coast when it debuted, and unusually it is built out over the water — about 40 feet of it hangs past the pier above Elliott Bay. It has 42 climate-controlled gondolas: 41 seating up to eight riders each, plus one VIP cabin for four.
seattle-great-wheel.descriptor: 175-foot Ferris wheel on Pier 57, built out over Elliott Bay

seattle-repertory-theatre.text: Seattle Rep was founded in 1963 in the Seattle Playhouse built for the 1962 World's Fair — actor Hal Holbrook is believed to be the person who suggested it as a home for a repertory company — and it won the Regional Theatre Tony Award in 1990. Its 673-seat Bagley Wright Theater at Seattle Center opened in October 1983, alongside the smaller 282-seat Leo K.
seattle-repertory-theatre.descriptor: Seattle Center resident theater company, founded 1963

seattle-yacht-club.text: The club's Opening Day Boat Parade runs through the Montlake Cut on the first Saturday in May, sharing the day with the Windermere Cup rowing races on the Lake Washington Ship Canal. Thousands line the Cut and the closed-to-traffic Montlake Bridge to watch the crews, then the parade that follows.
seattle-yacht-club.descriptor: Private yacht club on Portage Bay in Montlake

serafina.text: Susan Kaufman opened Serafina on Eastlake Ave in 1991, aiming for a neighborhood restaurant with the welcoming feel of an Italian home. Chef Christian Chandler first turned up as a culinary student on a mentorship, became co-owner in 2015, and took over as sole owner in 2019.
serafina.descriptor: Eastlake Ave Italian neighborhood restaurant since 1991

serious-pie.text: Tom Douglas's pizzeria bakes blistered thin crusts in a 600-degree stone-encased apple-wood-burning oven, with toppings that run to clams, nettles, soft egg and truffle cheese — the Yukon Gold potato pizza is the one people order. It has grown into arguably the most successful of his Seattle restaurant brands.
serious-pie.descriptor: Tom Douglas thin-crust, apple-wood-fired pizzeria downtown

shilshole-bay-marina.text: Completed in 1958 and run by the Port of Seattle, Shilshole is a 1,400-slip saltwater marina tucked behind a 4,000-foot breakwater, with a roughly mile-long public promenade facing the Olympic Mountains. Its Leif Erikson Plaza is marked by a 16-foot statue of the Norse explorer.
shilshole-bay-marina.descriptor: Port of Seattle saltwater marina in Seattle's Ballard neighborhood

shiros-sushi.text: Shiro Kashiba, who had already opened Seattle's first sushi counter, started this Belltown room in 1995 and built it on Edomae sushi — Tokyo technique applied to Puget Sound and Pacific Northwest fish like salmon, geoduck, oysters and albacore. He ran it for two decades before leaving to open Sushi Kashiba at Pike Place Market; chef Masaki Nishioka leads the kitchen now.
shiros-sushi.descriptor: Belltown Edomae sushi counter opened in 1995 by Shiro Kashiba

shortys.text: Shorty's is a Belltown dive on Second Avenue that bills itself as the ultimate Seattle pinball arcade bar, with a wall of machines, a trophy room, hot dogs and beer, and doors open from noon to 2am every day.
shortys.descriptor: Belltown pinball arcade bar at 2316 2nd Ave, hot dogs and beer

showbox-at-the-market.text: Open since July 1939, the Showbox has hosted Duke Ellington, Muddy Waters and the Ramones, and later the grunge era's Pearl Jam, Soundgarden and Mudhoney. When a developer floated a 42-story tower on the site in 2018, a petition drew more than 110,000 signatures, and in July 2019 Seattle's Landmarks Preservation Board voted unanimously to grant it landmark status.
showbox-at-the-market.descriptor: 1939 music hall on 1st Ave across from Pike Place Market, holds about 1,150

shuckers-oyster-bar.text: Shuckers sits in a preserved 1930s haberdashery inside the Olympic Hotel, which opened in December 1924 and was listed on the National Register in 1979 — the original tin ceiling and carved oak vignettes are still in place. Oysters come several ways, with live shucking of rotating Northwest varieties on Friday and Saturday evenings.
shuckers-oyster-bar.descriptor: Oyster bar in the Fairmont Olympic Hotel's 1930s haberdashery space

sky-view-observatory.text: The deck sits on the 73rd floor of the 933-foot Columbia Center, the tallest building in Washington since it was completed in 1985, and is described as the highest public viewing area west of the Mississippi River. It went from a 270-degree view to a full 360 degrees in 2013, with express elevators and a lounge added in 2018.
sky-view-observatory.descriptor: 73rd-floor observation deck atop the Columbia Center downtown

slims-last-chance.text: A Georgetown "chili shack and watering hole" built around four house chilis — Texas Red, brisket 'n bean, chili verde, and turkey with white beans — plus chili cheese fries, wings and a crawfish po-boy. Live music runs on two stages, one indoors and one outdoors.
slims-last-chance.descriptor: Georgetown chili shack and roadhouse bar with indoor and outdoor music stages

smith.text: Smith is the dark, wood-and-taxidermy bar on 15th Ave E — The Infatuation says the hunting-lodge look makes it feel like a lumberjack might walk in at any moment — known for burgers, bar snacks and cocktails, with everything in the kitchen made from scratch. Netflix's Love Is Blind used it as a date-night set in season four.
smith.descriptor: Taxidermy-lined bar and burger spot on 15th Ave E, Capitol Hill

smith-tower-observatory.text: Typewriter and firearms magnate L.C. Smith's 38-story tower opened in 1914 and stayed the tallest building west of the Mississippi for 17 years, until Kansas City passed it in 1931. The 35th-floor Chinese Room holds the carved Wishing Chair, and legend says an unmarried woman who sits in it will be married within the year. Tours resumed in 2016 alongside a Prohibition-themed bar.
smith-tower-observatory.descriptor: Observation deck and speakeasy bar on the 35th floor of the 1914 Smith Tower

space-needle.text: Built for the 1962 Century 21 Exposition, the 605-foot Needle was the tallest building west of the Mississippi until 1969 and was engineered to take 200 mph winds and a magnitude-9 earthquake on a foundation sunk 30 feet deep. Elevators reach the 520-foot observation deck in 41 seconds, and a 2018 renovation added a revolving glass floor where the old rotating restaurant used to spin.
space-needle.descriptor: 1962 World's Fair tower at Seattle Center, 605 feet tall

spud-fish-and-chips.text: The Alger brothers opened Spud across from Alki Beach in 1935, and it has been frying hand-filleted fish and fresh-cut chips there ever since; manager Carol Kelly marked 50 years behind the counter in 2022. One St. Patrick's Day a cook tinted the batter green — green fish, it turned out, did not sell.
spud-fish-and-chips.descriptor: Alki Beach fish-and-chips shack with hand-cut chips, since 1935

spud-fish-chips.text: Jack Alger opened this Green Lake Spud in 1940, five years after the Alger family's original on Alki Beach. It has moved several times around the lake over the decades — the latest, into a new and improved space, came in 2022 — but the hand-filleted fish and fresh-chopped spuds have stayed the same.
spud-fish-chips.descriptor: Green Lake fish-and-chips counter opened by Jack Alger in 1940

staple-fancy.text: Ethan Stowell's Ballard Avenue Italian room is built around one thing: a four-course Chef's Tasting Menu — small plates, pasta, a grilled entrée and dessert — that changes daily, is chosen by the kitchen rather than the table, and arrives family-style. Mondays run a cheaper version of the same feast.
staple-fancy.descriptor: Ethan Stowell Italian on Ballard Ave; four-course family-style chef's menu

storyville-coffee.text: Storyville started as a Bainbridge Island roaster in 2006 and put its flagship upstairs at First and Pike, on the top floor of the Corner Market building — in the space that for years housed the fine-dining restaurant Chez Shea. The company announced the Pike Place Market move in 2013 and still roasts on Bainbridge.
storyville-coffee.descriptor: Bainbridge-born roaster's cafe on the top floor of the Corner Market building

stoup-brewing.text: Brad Benson, Lara Zahaba and Robyn Schumacher left careers in forensic chemistry, wine marketing and high-school biology teaching to open Stoup in Ballard in 2013; Schumacher is a certified Cicerone. The NW 52nd St taproom pairs a wide beer list with a fire-pit beer garden and a different food truck most days.
stoup-brewing.descriptor: Ballard craft brewery and beer garden on NW 52nd, founded 2013

sushi-kappo-tamura.text: Chef Taichi Kitamura — who trained under Seattle sushi legend Shiro Kashiba — opened Tamura on Eastlake in 2010 with partner Steve Tamura, cooking kappo style in an open kitchen. The restaurant grows produce in a rooftop garden planted with the Seattle Urban Farm Company and sources from Northwest producers like Taylor Shellfish and Skagit River Ranch.
sushi-kappo-tamura.descriptor: Kappo-style sushi bar on Eastlake Ave with a rooftop garden, since 2010

sushi-kashiba.text: Shiro Kashiba, another chef mentored by Jiro Ono, opened Seattle's first sushi counter before founding Sushi Kashiba at Pike Place Market, where he serves edomae-style sushi with imported and local fish. In 2024 Japan awarded him the Order of the Rising Sun, Gold and Silver Rays, for promoting Japanese food culture abroad and training the next generation of chefs.
sushi-kashiba.descriptor: Edomae sushi counter on Pine St by Pike Place Market, chef Shiro Kashiba

t-mobile-park.text: The roof isn't a dome — it's a 22-million-pound umbrella covering about nine acres that leaves the sides open, so wind and cold still reach the field even when it's shut. Opened as Safeco Field in July 1999 and renamed T-Mobile Park in 2019, it hosted two perfect games in one season in 2012, including Félix Hernández's in August.
t-mobile-park.descriptor: Retractable-roof Mariners ballpark in SoDo, opened 1999

taco-time.text: Taco Time Northwest isn't the national chain — it's a separate, family-run Washington company that Frank Tonkin Sr. started in White Center in 1962 and that fourth-generation Tonkins still run across 77 Western Washington restaurants. Locals order the Crisp Burrito (about 3 million a year) and Tater-Fries, and the company has composted restaurant waste since 2012, diverting over 70% from landfills.
taco-time.descriptor: Northwest-only Taco Time; Crisp Burritos and Tater-Fries

tacos-chukis.text: Roberto Salmerón opened the first Tacos Chukis in 2011 in a tiny upstairs space on Capitol Hill, and it grew into a cult favorite for cheap, excellent tacos before expanding to South Lake Union, Beacon Hill and the Central District. The namesake "taco chukis" adds al pastor pork, cheese and grilled pineapple to the standard build.
tacos-chukis.descriptor: Cult Capitol Hill taqueria since 2011; al pastor tacos with cheese and pineapple

tai-tung-restaurant.text: Open at 655 S King St since 1935, Tai Tung is the oldest surviving Chinese restaurant in the Chinatown–International District, on the ground floor of the old Rex Hotel. Bruce Lee ate here as a young man, and the restaurant still points out his favorite back table and his usual order — oyster sauce beef and garlic shrimp.
tai-tung-restaurant.descriptor: Seattle's oldest Chinese restaurant, on S King St in the ID since 1935

tamarind-tree.text: Opened in late 2004 by Tam Nguyen, who came to the U.S. from a Malaysian refugee camp in 1980, Tamarind Tree is famously hard to find — the entrance is through a grungy parking lot it shares with Sichuanese Cuisine. Inside is a full provincial Vietnamese menu (bánh xèo, green papaya salad with prawns, grilled squid with ground pork) that Eater listed among Seattle's 38 essential restaurants.
tamarind-tree.descriptor: Provincial Vietnamese restaurant on S Jackson St, entered via a shared parking lot

tavern-law.text: Opened in 2009 by Brian McCracken and Dana Tough, Tavern Law is named for an 1832 law that legalized drinking in public houses. To reach Needle & Thread, the reservation-only bar upstairs, you pick up an antique telephone in the back corner and someone unlocks the vault door — there's no menu up there, the bartender builds a drink around your answers.
tavern-law.descriptor: Capitol Hill cocktail bar on 12th Ave with a hidden upstairs speakeasy

tavolata.text: Ethan Stowell's Tavolàta is built around a single long communal table running down the middle of an industrial, bi-level Belltown dining room on 2nd Ave. Handmade pasta is the whole point, and the carbonara is the dish reviewers keep singling out.
tavolata.descriptor: Ethan Stowell's handmade-pasta Italian room on 2nd Ave in Belltown

taylor-shellfish-farms.text: Taylor Shellfish is a fifth-generation family farm: an ancestor founded the Olympia Oyster Company in the 1890s, and the modern company was established in 1969 by brothers Edwin and Justin Taylor. It is the country's largest producer of farmed shellfish, and this is one of its Seattle oyster bars, shucking its own oysters, clams, mussels and geoduck a short walk from Seattle Center.
taylor-shellfish-farms.descriptor: Lower Queen Anne oyster bar run by a Puget Sound shellfish farm

taylor-shellfish-oyster-bar.text: The Taylor family has farmed Puget Sound shellfish since the 1890s, when a forebear founded the Olympia Oyster Company, and the company is now the country's largest producer of farmed shellfish. It began opening its own oyster bars in 2014; this Pioneer Square counter on Occidental Avenue serves their oysters, clams, mussels and geoduck straight off the farms.
taylor-shellfish-oyster-bar.descriptor: Raw bar on Occidental Ave in Pioneer Square from an 1890s oyster family

terra-plata.text: Terra Plata was chef Tamara Murphy's restaurant with co-owner Linda Di Lello Morton, cooking Spanish-influenced shared plates from organic and sustainably farmed ingredients at 1501 Melrose Ave. Murphy won the James Beard Award for Best Chef in the Pacific Northwest and Hawaii in 1995; she died in August 2024, and Di Lello Morton has carried the restaurant on. The heated, covered rooftop garden terrace runs year-round and Mondays are paella night.
terra-plata.descriptor: Spanish-influenced shared plates with a rooftop garden terrace on Melrose Ave

thai-siam.text: One of north Seattle's longest-running Thai kitchens — the restaurant has been serving on this stretch of 15th Ave NW, just north of Ballard, since 1987.
thai-siam.descriptor: Thai restaurant on 15th Ave NW north of Ballard, serving since 1987

thai-tom.text: A tiny University Way storefront where the cooking happens on woks right behind the counter, so watching it is part of the meal — the closest thing Seattle has to a Bangkok street stall. Cash only, no cards.
thai-tom.descriptor: Cash-only Thai counter on The Ave with the woks in plain view

thats-amore-italian-cafe.text: That's Amore has served pasta, pizza and calzones since 1994 out of a 1920s brick building on 31st Ave S that was once the Mount Baker Pharmacy, with Seattle skyline views from about fourteen tables. Guy Devillier and David Hoefer bought the neighborhood spot in 2018.
thats-amore-italian-cafe.descriptor: Italian cafe in Mount Baker with skyline views, open since 1994

the-5-point.text: Open since 1929 and running 24 hours, the 5 Point is the oldest drinking establishment in Belltown; its neon signs read "Alcoholics serving alcoholics since 1929" and "We cheat tourists-n-drunks since 1929." Dick Smith, who took over the bar from his father in 1975, installed a periscope above the men's-room urinal aimed at the Space Needle, which is still the bar's most-repeated bit of lore.
the-5-point.descriptor: 24-hour Belltown dive bar and diner, open since 1929

the-athenian-seafood-restaurant-and-bar.text: The Athenian has been at 1517 Pike Place since 1909 and was among the first businesses in Seattle to pick up a beer license in 1933, as Prohibition ended. Film fans know it as a Sleepless in Seattle (1993) shooting location.
the-athenian-seafood-restaurant-and-bar.descriptor: Pike Place Market seafood restaurant and bar, open since 1909

writtenFor.name: The Athenian Seafood Restaurant and Bar

the-boat.text: Phở Bắc began in 1982 in the Chinatown–International District as Cat's Submarine Sandwich Shop; phở caught on so fast the owners renamed the place within four months. Its 12th and Jackson location is known simply as The Boat, after the red hull-shaped building it moved into — originally a float built for a 2004 parade by Seattle's Vietnamese Catholic community. Owners Yenvy and Quynh-Vy Pham were James Beard restaurateur semifinalists in 2023.
the-boat.descriptor: Phở in the red boat-shaped building at 12th & Jackson, Little Saigon

the-central-saloon.text: Opened in 1892, the Central is one of Seattle's oldest saloons and a Pioneer Square rock landmark: Nirvana played their first Seattle show in this room, a gig that led to the band signing with Sub Pop, and much of the early grunge scene, Soundgarden included, came through behind them. The owners bought the building outright in 2022, taking it off the redevelopment table.
the-central-saloon.descriptor: Pioneer Square dive bar and live-music venue, open since 1892

the-crumpet-shop.text: Open in the Corner Market building at First and Pike Place since 1976, the Crumpet Shop griddles its own crumpets and tops them sweet or savory — ricotta and honey, ham and egg, or the "Seattle-style" one with smoked salmon and cucumber. The shop has been handed from one family to the next over the decades.
the-crumpet-shop.descriptor: Crumpets and tea at 1st & Pike in Pike Place Market since 1976

the-electric-lady-studio-guitar.text: Daryl Smith's life-size bronze of Jimi Hendrix — down on his knees, mid-solo with a Stratocaster — has stood at Broadway and Pine since 1997. It came from an "alternative corporate art collection" of musician statues (Chuck Berry, Buddy Holly, Elvis among them) commissioned by AEI Music founder Michael J. Malone; Hunters Capital owns and maintains them now. Vandals tagged it in 2013 on the 43rd anniversary of Hendrix's death.
the-electric-lady-studio-guitar.descriptor: Life-size bronze Jimi Hendrix statue at Broadway and Pine, Capitol Hill

the-harvest-vine.text: The Harvest Vine grew out of a catering business: opened in 1998 by Carolin Messier and a former partner as a small specialty food shop, it became a 16-seat restaurant on E Madison once neighbors wanted to stay for dinner. Three expansions later it seats 74, still cooking Spanish and Basque food, with Joey Serquinia as executive chef since 2008.
the-harvest-vine.descriptor: Basque-Spanish tapas on E Madison in Madison Valley since 1998

the-loupe-lounge.text: The Loupe Lounge sits atop what the Space Needle bills as the world's first and only revolving glass floor, added in the tower's $100 million renovation completed in August 2018. The floor takes about 45 minutes to complete one rotation, so the cocktails and local beer and wine come with a slowly turning view straight down at Seattle.
the-loupe-lounge.descriptor: Walk-up cocktail bar on the Space Needle's revolving glass floor level

the-nest-at-thompson-seattle.text: A 21-and-over rooftop bar on top of the Thompson Seattle at 110 Stewart Street, overlooking Pike Place Market, serving craft cocktails with open-air views out over Elliott Bay.
the-nest-at-thompson-seattle.descriptor: Rooftop cocktail bar atop the Thompson Seattle on Stewart Street

the-pine-box.text: The Pine Box pours craft beer and pizza inside an old mortuary chapel on Melrose Avenue, and leans all the way into it — the bar's own line is "Ashes to ashes, crust to crust."
the-pine-box.descriptor: Craft beer bar and pizzeria in a former Capitol Hill mortuary chapel

the-pink-door.text: Jackie Roberts opened the Pink Door in 1981 and never put up a sign — you find it by spotting the pink door in Post Alley below Pike Place Market. Four decades on it's a Market fixture, serving Italian-American food from family recipes with produce sourced almost exclusively from Butler Farms, across the water on Bainbridge Island.
the-pink-door.descriptor: Italian-American restaurant behind an unmarked pink door in Post Alley

the-quad.text: Thirty Yoshino cherry trees ring the University of Washington's Liberal Arts Quadrangle. They were bought in 1939 and planted at the Washington Park Arboretum, then transplanted to campus in 1962 when SR 520 construction displaced them. Between mid-March and early April the bloom pulls crowds into the quad, whose layout was set in 1915 by UW president Henry Suzzallo and architect Carl Gould.
the-quad.descriptor: University of Washington's main quad, famous for its cherry blossoms

the-seattle-public-library-central-libra.text: Rem Koolhaas and Joshua Prince-Ramus's 11-story glass-and-steel library opened in May 2004 and pulled 2.3 million visitors in its first year, roughly a third from outside Seattle. Its Books Spiral runs the nonfiction collection up a continuous ramp across four floors so the Dewey Decimal sequence never breaks across shelves. Bill Gates gave $20 million toward the $165.9 million building.

writtenFor.name: The Seattle Public Library - Central Library

the-sunset-tavern.text: Max Genereaux built a stage inside a Ballard Avenue storefront that had been a Chinese restaurant from the 1940s through the 1970s, and opened the Sunset in 2000. The roughly 200-capacity room has hosted Mudhoney and Fleet Foxes, and it claims the cleanest bathrooms in rock and roll — walls decoupaged with everything from fluffy kittens to postcards.
the-sunset-tavern.descriptor: Ballard Ave live-music dive in a former mid-century Chinese restaurant

the-triple-door.text: The Triple Door occupies the Mann building at 216 Union Street, home to the Embassy Theatre, which opened in 1925 and stayed a popular movie house into the fifties. It closed in 1984, the year a pipe bomb damaged the building as a diversion for a robbery. Rick and Ann Yoder bought it in 1999 and opened the venue in September 2003 as a 250-seat main stage with the 50-seat Musicquarium lounge.
the-triple-door.descriptor: Downtown dinner-and-music venue in the old Embassy Theatre

the-vera-project.text: The Vera Project's first show, on January 27, 2001, drew close to 1,000 people for the Murder City Devils, Botch and the Blood Brothers. Founded that year by James Keblas, Shannon Stewart and Kate Becker and modeled on an all-ages club in Groningen, Netherlands, it's an all-ages nonprofit at Seattle Center that teaches 14-to-24-year-olds audio engineering, screen printing and show production. It moved into its permanent home there in 2007.
the-vera-project.descriptor: All-ages nonprofit music and arts venue at Seattle Center

the-walrus-and-the-carpenter.text: Chef Renee Erickson opened this Ballard Avenue oyster bar in 2010, and it has become one of Seattle's best-known seafood rooms - nominated for the James Beard Foundation's Outstanding Restaurant award in 2022 and a regular on Seattle Metropolitan's best-seafood lists.
the-walrus-and-the-carpenter.descriptor: Renee Erickson's oyster bar on Ballard Avenue, open since 2010

the-wayward-cafe.text: The Wayward traces its roots to 1996 and a cafe near the University of Washington called Good Morning Healing Earth; it later became the Wayward Vegan Cafe and now runs as an entirely plant-based diner in Roosevelt. It's a long-standing Seattle vegan standby, with a Yelp top-100 vegan burger nod and Seattle Times gold-winner honors in 2023, 2024 and 2025.
the-wayward-cafe.descriptor: All-vegan diner on NE 65th St in Roosevelt: burgers, breakfast, comfort food

the-wing-dome.text: The Wing Dome has been frying wings in Seattle since 1994, and the reason people make the trip to Greenwood is the 7-Alarm Challenge: seven of the hottest wings in seven minutes, no drinks, no napkins, hands licked clean, waiver signed. Finish and your photo goes on the Wall of Flame; fail and it costs you $7.77.
the-wing-dome.descriptor: Hot-wing joint on Greenwood Ave N with a 7-Alarm eating challenge

tilikum-place-cafe.text: The cafe takes its name from the little triangular plaza out front, where James Wehn's life-size statue of Chief Seattle stands — "Tilikum" is Chinook Jargon for "people" or "friend," and the site marks where the land claims of Seattle pioneers Denny, Bell and Boren converged. The kitchen is a Belltown brunch spot, best known for powdered-sugar-dusted Dutch babies.
tilikum-place-cafe.descriptor: Belltown brunch cafe known for its Dutch babies, on Tilikum Place

top-pot-doughnuts.text: Brothers Mark and Michael Klebeck started Top Pot on Capitol Hill in 2002 after buying a vintage neon sign from a shuttered Chinese restaurant called Topspot. The "S" fell off in transit, and Mark suggested replacing it with a coffee pot — hence the name. The 5th Avenue store is the flagship, roasts its own coffee, and drew President Obama for a doughnut run in October 2010.
top-pot-doughnuts.descriptor: Doughnut shop and coffee roaster on 5th Ave; the chain's downtown flagship

toulouse-petit.text: Toulouse Petit brings French Quarter cooking to Lower Queen Anne — BBQ shrimp and grits, crab Benedict, house-made charcuterie — in a Cajun-Creole kitchen and lounge. Locally it's best known for the happy hour: fifty-plus small plates, run twice a day, late afternoon and again late at night.
toulouse-petit.descriptor: Cajun-Creole kitchen on Queen Anne Ave with a twice-daily happy hour

tutta-bella-neapolitan-pizzeria.text: Joe Fugere opened the first Tutta Bella in Columbia City in January 2004, and it became the first restaurant in the Pacific Northwest certified by Naples' Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana — which dictates tipo 00 flour, San Marzano tomatoes, fior di latte and a wood-fired dome oven. Tutta Bella also made a pizza called "Il Presidente" that was served aboard Air Force One during a Barack Obama visit.
tutta-bella-neapolitan-pizzeria.descriptor: Certified Neapolitan pizzeria on Stone Way in Wallingford

umi-sake-house.text: A First Avenue izakaya in Belltown built around a sake list of more than 60 imported Japanese bottles, with two happy hours a day — the late one running from 10pm to close, which is why it's a standard after-work and after-show stop.
umi-sake-house.descriptor: Belltown izakaya and sushi house with 60+ imported Japanese sakes

un-bien.text: Brothers Julian and Lucas Lorenzo opened Un Bien in June 2015 to carry on the sandwich their father had made at his shop Paseo. The draw is the same one: the Caribbean Roast, slow-roasted marinated pork shoulder on a toasted Macrina baguette with aioli, cilantro, pickled jalapeños and caramelized onions. Yelp named it Washington's best restaurant in 2016.
un-bien.descriptor: Caribbean sandwich counter on 15th Ave NW known for the Caribbean Roast

underground-tour.text: The Great Seattle Fire of June 6, 1889 leveled the wooden downtown. As the city rebuilt, it raised Pioneer Square's street grades by up to a story to fix drainage and steep terrain, leaving the old sidewalks and shopfronts sealed in areaways underneath. Bill Speidel started leading tours of those passages in 1965, and they still set out from the Pioneer Building.
underground-tour.descriptor: Guided walk through Pioneer Square's buried 1890s sidewalks and storefronts

via-tribunali-capitol-hill.text: Via Tribunali opened in a former Capitol Hill auto body shop in 2004. Its wood-burning brick oven was built entirely from materials shipped from Naples — including bricks made with Mt. Vesuvius ash — and assembled by a Neapolitan master craftsman brought over for the job. The pizzeria is a member of the Verace Pizza Napoletana association.
via-tribunali-capitol-hill.descriptor: Neapolitan pizzeria on Capitol Hill with a Naples-built wood-fired oven

victor-steinbrueck-park.text: The 0.8-acre lawn sits on the site of a National Guard armory that was demolished in 1968; it was landscaped as "Market Park" in 1982 and renamed in 1985 for Victor Steinbrueck, the architect and preservationist who fought for Pike Place Market and Pioneer Square. Its two cedar totem poles went up in March 1984, and the park reopened in March 2025 after a long renovation.
victor-steinbrueck-park.descriptor: Grassy overlook beside Pike Place Market with Elliott Bay views

victrola-coffee-roasters.text: Victrola started roasting in 2000, and its flagship on East Pike doubles as cafe, roastery, training facility and cupping room inside a 1920s Auto Row building. Epicurious named it one of the 25 best coffee shops in the U.S., singling out the free public cuppings of its single-origin coffees.
victrola-coffee-roasters.descriptor: Cafe and roastery in a 1920s Auto Row building on E Pike St, est. 2000

writtenFor.name: Victrola Coffee Roasters - Capitol Hill (East Pike Street)

virginia-inn.text: The Virginia Inn opened in 1903 in the Hotel Livingston at First and Virginia — four years before Pike Place Market itself. The old tavern has shown up on film in both Singles and Sleepless in Seattle, and it survived a 2025 lease scare that nearly ended its run after more than 120 years.
virginia-inn.descriptor: Bar and restaurant at 1st & Virginia, open since 1903

virginia-v.text: The Virginia V is the last operating steamer of Puget Sound's "Mosquito Fleet," the small boats that moved people and freight around the Sound before highways. Launched in 1922, she carried Camp Fire Girls to Camp Sealth on Vashon Island until 1970 and beat the Grayline Sightseer in a 1948 publicity race. A National Historic Landmark since 1992, she's moored at Lake Union Park after a $6.5 million restoration.
virginia-v.descriptor: 1922 steamship at Lake Union Park; last of the Mosquito Fleet

volunteer-park.text: John Charles Olmsted of the Olmsted Brothers laid the park out along the ridgetop in 1903, and the city renamed it from City Park to honor Spanish-American War volunteers. You can take in the view from the 1906 water tower's observation deck, walk the 1912 conservatory that arrived as a kit from New York, and look through Isamu Noguchi's granite "Black Sun" (1969) toward the Space Needle. The park hosted Seattle's first Gay Pride Week in 1974.
volunteer-park.descriptor: Olmsted-designed Capitol Hill park with a conservatory and 1906 water tower

volunteer-park-water-tower.text: Built by the Water Department in 1906, the brick tower stands next to the highest point on Capitol Hill — 444 feet above sea level — and has an observation deck near the top. The park around it was laid out by John Charles Olmsted of the Olmsted Brothers firm, hired in 1903 as part of Seattle's park and boulevard system.
volunteer-park-water-tower.descriptor: 1906 brick water tower with an observation deck in Volunteer Park

vons-1000-spirits.text: Von's 1000 Spirits is named for the Firnstahl family's spirits collection, which traces back to the Guinness world record their old Jake O'Shaughnessy's saloon set for the world's largest collection of fine spirits. Tim Firnstahl co-founded that 1974 saloon before opening Von's; today the 1st Avenue kitchen is known for its house sourdough and handcrafted cocktails.
vons-1000-spirits.descriptor: Downtown bar and restaurant on 1st Ave built around a big spirits collection

voulas-offshore-cafe.text: A Lake Union breakfast counter on NE Northlake Way by the University Bridge, where the scrambles come with Greek sausage and feta — the Greek Hobo, and among the omelettes the Freagy Greegy. Guy Fieri's Food Network visit left its mark on the menu, which still carries a "Guy Fieri's Choices" omelette section led by the Oddinator: house-smoked pork, mushrooms, green onions and Swiss under BBQ sauce.
voulas-offshore-cafe.descriptor: Greek-run breakfast diner on NE Northlake Way by the University Bridge

washington-park-arboretum.text: The 230-acre arboretum was established in 1934 and is run jointly by the University of Washington, Seattle Parks and Recreation and the Arboretum Foundation, on grounds the Olmsted Brothers designed after the city acquired the land in 1900. Azalea Way, its signature spring walk, follows the line of a former horse racing track, and Eleanor Roosevelt planted an elm here on a 1938 visit.
washington-park-arboretum.descriptor: 230-acre UW-run arboretum with Azalea Way and a Japanese garden

waterfront-park.text: The first Waterfront Park opened in 1974 on the site of Schwabacher Wharf — the pier where the steamship Portland landed with a ton of Alaska gold in 1897 and touched off the rush that made Seattle the gateway north. The pier closed in 2020 and its central section collapsed during demolition; the rebuilt park opened September 6, 2025 with a lawn and a playground around an 18-foot jellyfish structure.
waterfront-park.descriptor: Rebuilt downtown waterfront park on Alaskan Way at Pier 58

westlake-park.text: Seattle's de facto town square was proposed in 1968 and took two decades and a stack of lawsuits to build, finally opening in October 1988. Its granite pavers cracked almost immediately — a design flaw locals dubbed the "Nightmare on Pine Street" that ended in a $515,000 settlement. Generations of rallies and speeches happened here before a 2025-26 renovation removed the fountain and arch.
westlake-park.descriptor: Downtown plaza at Pine & 4th, Seattle's de facto town square

westmans-bagel-and-coffee.text: Westman's started in 2018 as a Capitol Hill walk-up window from restaurateur Monica Dimas and baker Molly Westman, a tribute to classic New York City deli culture. Every bagel is cold-fermented, hand-rolled and boiled before it's baked each morning. It has since grown to three shops and is now owned by Sanya and Ankit Sirmorya.
westmans-bagel-and-coffee.descriptor: NYC-style bagels and coffee; the original Capitol Hill shop on E Madison

westmans-bagel-coffee.text: The U District outpost of a bagel shop that began in 2018 as a Capitol Hill walk-up window run by restaurateur Monica Dimas and baker Molly Westman. The bagels are cold-fermented, hand-rolled and boiled before baking each morning, with locally roasted Caffe Vita espresso alongside.
westmans-bagel-coffee.descriptor: NYC-style bagel and coffee counter on the Ave in the U District

westward.text: Chef Josh Henderson opened Westward in 2013 on the north shore of Lake Union; after a 2018 sale it is run by Renée Erickson's Sea Creatures group, serving Northwest seafood with a Mediterranean twist. Adirondack chairs and a fire pit on the waterfront deck face the lake and skyline, and you can tie up a boat out front.
westward.descriptor: Waterfront seafood restaurant on north Lake Union with a fire pit and boat dock

wild-ginger-seattle.text: Rick and Ann Yoder came home from a trip through Southeast Asia in 1989 and opened Wild Ginger to bring those flavors to Seattle. The kitchen serves a family-style tour of China and Southeast Asia, and the restaurant has since grown to three locations around the region.
wild-ginger-seattle.descriptor: Pan-Asian dining room on 3rd Ave downtown, open since 1989

wildrose.text: Started by a collective of five women in the mid-1980s, the Wildrose was deliberately built with big street-facing windows at a time when most queer bars in Seattle kept their entrances hidden. It is named for Montana wildflowers, and it is now the city's only lesbian bar — the owners bill it as the oldest in the country.
wildrose.descriptor: Capitol Hill lesbian bar on E Pike St, "celebrating love since 1984"

wing-luke-asian-museum.text: Founded in 1967 in memory of Wing Luke, the first Asian American elected to public office in the Pacific Northwest, who died in a 1965 plane crash. Since 2008 it has occupied the 1910 East Kong Yick Building, financed by 170 Chinese immigrants — the only pan-Asian Pacific American community-based museum in the country, a Smithsonian affiliate and a National Park Service affiliated area.
wing-luke-asian-museum.descriptor: Asian Pacific American art and history museum on S King St in the Chinatown-ID

woodland-park.text: The park was lumber-mill owner Guy Phinney's private estate, and the small menagerie he kept there grew into Woodland Park Zoo. After his death his widow sold the 188 acres to Seattle in 1899 for $5,000 cash plus a $95,000 mortgage — over the mayor's veto — and the Olmsted Brothers were hired in 1902 to design it. Aurora Avenue was later cut straight through, splitting the park in two.
woodland-park.descriptor: 90-acre Phinney Ridge park split by Aurora Ave, beside the zoo and Green Lake

woodland-park-zoo.text: The zoo grew out of the private menagerie on lumber-mill owner Guy Phinney's estate; the city bought the 188-acre property from his widow in 1899 for $5,000 plus assumption of a $95,000 mortgage. In 1975 director David Hancocks reinvented zoo design here with 'landscape immersion,' putting animals in replicas of their natural habitats — starting with the gorillas, and the idea spread worldwide.
woodland-park-zoo.descriptor: 92-acre zoo in Seattle's Phinney Ridge neighborhood, city-owned since 1899

xian-noodles.text: Lily Wu opened the first Xi'an Noodles in the U District in May 2016 and added this Westlake Center location in 2019, serving hand-pulled biangbiang noodles, spicy tingly beef and malatang. Seattle Metropolitan called her biangbiang noodles the best version in city limits — the room is plain and nobody comes for the decor.
xian-noodles.descriptor: Hand-pulled biangbiang noodles at Westlake Center downtown

zig-zag-cafe.text: Tucked into the 1910 Fix-Madore Building on the Pike Street Hill Climb, Zig Zag is where bartender Murray Stenson (here 2002-2011) revived the Last Word, a forgotten Prohibition-era cocktail he found in 2004 in a 1952 copy of Ted Saucier's "Bottom's Up!" It spread from this bar to cocktail menus nationwide, and GQ called Zig Zag the nation's best cocktail bar in 2010.
zig-zag-cafe.descriptor: Hidden cocktail bar on the Pike Street Hill Climb below the Market

zoka-coffee-greenlake.text: Zoka roasted its first batch in fall 1996 and opened this Green Lake cafe — its first — on January 7, 1997; founder Jeff Babcock still runs the company. Its beans are roasted on a 1963 German Probat, and Zoka baristas took national barista championships in 2002 and 2005 before Roast magazine named it Macro Roaster of the Year in 2008.
zoka-coffee-greenlake.descriptor: Original Zoka coffeehouse and roaster by Green Lake, open since 1997
